extracted.intended_audience: parliamentarians, legislative drafters, agency officials, administrative law practitioners, and public policy makers
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance and procedural standards for independent administrative agencies on how to formulate statutory mandates, subordinate legislation, rule‑making and participatory processes (notice-and-comment) to promote accountability, fairness, effectiveness and comprehensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authoritativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Making decisions that are accorded full recognition. Where authority is ostensibly given to an agency to decide a matter, those who deal with the agency are entitled to have the decision made by the agency, not by a politician, judge or other decision maker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should exercise the decision‑making power granted to them so that their decisions receive full recognition and are not displaced by external actors. Excessive executive or judicial intervention can undermine an agency's authoritativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Making the administrative process as understandable as possible to those whom it affects; interested persons must know whom to address, about what matters, and how to address them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes, regulations and agency procedures should be drafted and organized to make agency objectives, contacts and procedures transparent. Minimizing unnecessary diversity in rules and adopting consistent formats or model provisions improves system comprehensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness, Economy and Efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: "Getting the job done" without wasting human and material resources; administration demands constant attentiveness to new and better ways of doing things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural design should balance thoroughness with speed and resource constraints. Where possible, subordinate legislation and procedural rule‑making should enable agencies to be dynamic and responsive while preserving necessary process values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: According appropriate recognition to the interests that may be affected by agency decisions; fairness generates trust, credibility and the co‑operation essential for efficient administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures (notice, hearings, access to information) should be designed to give affected parties a meaningful opportunity to be heard. Overlooking fairness risks loss of legitimacy and cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Operating in a manner true to the objectives laid down for the agency; having a full commitment to its purposes and being sufficiently free of background pressures to project competence and confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should safeguard independence from improper background pressures and adopt practices that demonstrate fidelity to statutory purposes. Integrity reinforces public and stakeholder respect for the agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness
rubrics_metrics.description: Making the administrative process accessible to those it affects and providing a window through which it can be seen; openness is a further guarantee of fairness and accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish agendas, consultative documents, and make information available so that affected persons can participate meaningfully. Openness supports scrutiny and enhances legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principled Decision Making
rubrics_metrics.description: Rationally correlating the information the agency has, the interests of which it is aware, and the objectives, policies and criteria that are to guide its decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions should be based on explained criteria linking evidence, interests and statutory objectives; avoid ad hoc policy formulation that cannot be justified by the agency's stated criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance the public interest while respecting private interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must not merely resolve private disputes; they must also advance the public interest, having due regard for private interests, in a way that will promote optimal voluntary compliance with the policy that is adopted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and decision‑making should balance public goals with private rights to encourage compliance; failure to consider both can undermine policy effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common legislated standards as basis for procedural framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Importance of common legislated standards as the basis of a more rational procedural framework to make agencies more accountable and to balance fairness with effectiveness, economy and efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt common procedural norms (notice, hearing, access to information) across agencies where practicable so stakeholders can expect consistent treatment and agencies can operate within a predictable regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize unnecessary diversity in agency procedural rules
rubrics_metrics.description: An approach to procedure that would minimize unnecessary diversity in the rules that agencies adopt, thus improving the comprehensibility of the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use model provisions, checklists and consistent drafting practices to reduce needless variation between constituent Acts and agency procedures; avoid bespoke complexity without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and particularity of statutory mandates
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever Parliament creates an agency or alters its responsibilities, it should state as clearly as possible, in plain and unambiguous language, the broad objectives the agency is to pursue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid obscure, confusing or unduly broad mandates that produce uncertainty as to goals and enforcement. A useful test is that objectives afford sufficient particularity to allow someone to disagree. Poorly defined mandates invite uneven enforcement, litigation, and difficulty in evaluating agency performance. (Example: criticism of overly broad mandates such as s.3 of the National Transportation Act.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave scope for development of complementary administrative policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament should leave sufficient scope for the development of complementary administrative policy as the agency gains experience, provided policy evolves in an orderly and open fashion and consistent with the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation need not be exhaustive; subordinate legislation and agency rule‑making can elaborate detail. The key is orderly, transparent development with accountability mechanisms and periodic review of constituent Acts to avoid unacceptable gaps between stated and applied policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary assent for substantive transfers of duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliamentary approval should be required through an affirmative resolution procedure whenever authority is used to transfer duties to and from agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While minor transfers may be impractical to legislate, transfers that materially redefine an agency's role should carry formal parliamentary scrutiny to reflect the seriousness of such interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent drafting format and early involvement of legislative drafters
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament should try to adopt a consistent format wherever broadly analogous objectives are contemplated for different agencies; early involvement of legislative drafters and use of checklists and model provisions improves comprehensibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences in timing, drafters and political context produce incongruities; using standard formats and checklists mitigates this and supports clearer constituent Acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use subordinate legislation to foster equality, accountability and comprehensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Subordinate legislation can foster equality of treatment in similar circumstances and can give interested persons a better insight into the motivations of the decision maker; properly used it promotes accountability, comprehensibility and fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where agencies have policy and regulatory functions, subordinate legislation can be an effective vehicle to set durable objectives while retaining necessary flexibility. It also creates opportunities for public participation at the policy development stage (e.g., regulatory agendas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of regulatory agendas and consultative documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication of a regulatory agenda and issuance of consultative documents containing proposals for new regulations, safety criteria, etc., broaden participation and raise expectations about consultation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory agendas should identify initiatives, state the problem, legal authority, availability of socio‑economic analysis, and a departmental contact. Consultative documents (as used by Atomic Energy Control Board, NEB, CHRC) invite written replies and sometimes meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of reasonable participation (notice-and-comment) in subordinate legislative process
rubrics_metrics.description: To be 'reasonable' the opportunity to participate should be genuine, commensurate with the importance of the issue, open, equally available to competing interests, and sufficiently early in the process to be meaningful without crippling the agency with unreasonable delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure participation is substantive not ceremonial; consider offsetting participation costs through direct funding, cost awards (as by CRTC), economic support to legal service groups, or government representation of constituent interests via advocacy officers. Participation should broaden perspective, improve fairness and efficiency, and enhance legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ceremonial or pre‑emptive consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice and comment processes should not become ceremonial or be preceded by pre‑decisions that vitiate meaningful participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Canada Post decided on the practical definition of "letter" before undertaking the statutory notice and comment process — a cautionary example. Agencies should avoid fixing key policy details before public consultation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate legislation appropriate where mandates mix policy with decision‑making
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an independent administrative agency is given a mandate that mixes policy elaboration with a decision‑making role, subordinate legislation is a useful means of structuring and communicating that policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize contexts (e.g., specialized adjudicative functions) where subordinate legislation may be inappropriate; choose the instrument suited to the function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing, scrutiny and publication requirements for regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Statutory Instruments Act, regulations must be filed in advance with the Clerk of the Privy Council who, with the Deputy Minister of Justice, scrutinizes them for vires, unusual use of authority, undue encroachment on the rights of individuals, and quality of drafting; regulations are subsequently registered and published and referred to the Standing Joint Committee for scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure advance review of regulations for legal authority, human rights impact and drafting quality; maintain registration and publication to promote transparency and parliamentary oversight (quality, vires, human rights, and merits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance elected accountability with participatory legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Too much emphasis on elected accountability as the sole source of legitimacy for public policy making should be counterbalanced by offering reasonable opportunities for interested persons to participate in subordinate legislative processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participation provides an alternative source of legitimacy and encourages agencies' policy‑making initiative; do not treat participation as a substitute for parliamentary accountability but as a complement.
